Test file: src/claim-office.spec.ts
Failing test: "should charge 165G for a newcomer's cursed steel sword with enchantment 3"
Current error: AssertionError: expected 170 to be 165
Implementation file: src/claim-office.ts

The spec's two integration examples establish the correct premium model. Policy-level percentage modifiers apply to the POLICY BASE PREMIUM (the sum of unmodified item base premiums), NOT to the item-surcharge-inflated amount. Item-level surcharges are added on top.

Example 1: cursed sword, enchantment 3, 0 years, first contract.
  100 base + 50 curse + 10 first insurance (10% of 100) = 160, + 5 fee = 165.
Example 2: cursed sword, enchantment 7, 3 years, second contract.
  100 base + 50 curse + 30 high ench - 20 loyalty + 10 first - 15 follow-up = 155, + 5 fee = 160.
  (policy modifiers net -25% of the base 100 = -25)

So: premium = ceil(policyBasePremium + itemSurcharges + policyBasePremium * policyPercentageDelta / 100 + fee)
where policyPercentageDelta is the NET signed percentage (+10 first, -20 loyalty when years >= 2, -15 when previousContracts >= 1).

IMPORTANT: this corrects the model, so several existing expectations were computed under the old (wrong) multiplicative model and must be recomputed from the spec. In particular the test "should add a 50% surcharge on a cursed item's base premium" currently expects 170 for the same scenario and must become 165. Recompute EVERY currently-passing expectation under the corrected model and update those that change. Verify each old value before replacing it, and list every expectation you changed with its old and new value.

Note the component block: a block of 3 prices at a flat 60 base premium. Treat that 60 as base premium for policy-modifier purposes.

EXPERIMENT MODE: Run autonomously, proceed to Refactor after completion.

content.text:
All 27 active tests pass.

Green Phase Complete:

**Implementation** (`/home/experimenter/experiments/runs/2026-07-26_09-57-57_claim-office-example-mapping_v4-exact-subagents_opus-5-no-thinking/src/claim-office.ts`): Split the premium calculation into two separate additive terms instead of one multiplicative chain. `premiumOf` (base × (1 + itemRate)) became `sumBasePremiums` + `sumItemSurcharges`; `policyPercentageOf` (which returned 100 + delta) became `policyPercentageDeltaOf` (signed delta only, dropping the now-unused `FULL_PERCENTAGE`); `premiumOfGroup` became `basePremiumOfGroup`, so a 3-item block contributes its flat 60 as base premium and its members' surcharges flow through `sumItemSurcharges` over the whole item list. `quote` now computes `ceil(policyBase + itemSurcharges + policyBase * delta / 100 + fee)`.

**Result**: 27 passed, 28 todo.

**Approach**: This is the minimal change that expresses the corrected model — the existing group/type/percentage helpers were reused as-is, and no behaviour beyond the two integration examples was added.

**Expectations recomputed** (5 changed, all in the item-modifier area where the old multiplicative model inflated the policy-modifier base; every other active expectation was verified to be unchanged because it has zero item surcharges, so the two models coincide):

| Test | Old | New |
|---|---|---|
| should add a 50% surcharge on a cursed item's base premium | 170 | 165 |
| should add a 30% surcharge for an item with enchantment exactly 5 | 148 | 145 |
| should add both surcharges for an item that is cursed and enchantment >= 5 | 203 | 195 |
| should apply the cursed surcharge only to the cursed item's base premium, not the policy total | 236 | 231 |
| should charge 165G for a newcomer's cursed steel sword with enchantment 3 (target) | 170 (actual) | 165 |

Unchanged and re-verified: all 8 base-premium tests, all 6 component-block tests, the enchantment-4 test (115), all 6 policy-level tests (115 / 95 / 115 / 100 / 115 / 80), and the rounding test (198).

One cross-check worth flagging: the still-todo integration example 2 (cursed sword, enchantment 7, 3 years, second contract) computes to **160** under this implementation, matching the spec — so the model is confirmed by both integration examples, not just the one being made green.
